The mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of the Qin dynasty, is a broad, flat-topped pyramid said to have been 76 meters high when intact.

Although numerous, the pyramids of the US are invariably small-scale burial mausoleums, built for wealthy patrons mostly between 1890-1920 (with the notable exception of actor Nicolas Cage's future tomb, constructed in the 2010s).

The Shard is a pyramid-shaped 72-story skyscraper located in London, England and completed in 2013.
The centerpiece of the exterior of Paris' famed art museum, the Louvre, is a glass pyramid nearly 21 meters high.

Italy has one historically significant pyramid, the Pyramid of Cestius in Rome. Built around 18–12 BCE as a tomb for Gaius Cestius, it reflects Egyptian influence on Roman architecture and remains an important landmark.

Known as the Nubian Pyramids, Sudan's pyramids are smaller, newer, and more numerous than the Egyptian pyramids that inspired them. The cemeteries at Meroë alone are said to contain as many as 147 pyramids.

Peru has many pre-Columbian pyramid-like structures along its coastal valleys, built by successive cultures for ceremonial, religious, and administrative purposes. Sites like Túcume, Huaca Pucllana, and Caral‑Supe represent the most historically significant pyramids.
The yet-unfinished (as of 2023) Ryugyong Hotel features a central column and large, triangular vanes that give the building a triangular/pyramidal shape.

Koh Ker is a layered pyramid at the ancient Khmer capital Lingapura, featuring monumental stone constructions, influencing later Khmer architecture, and used for ceremonial and administrative purposes.

Ireland's pyramids are all small-scale, comparatively modern constructions, the eldest of which was erected in 1760. They typically serve as burial mausoleums.
Most pyramids in Belize and other mesoamerican locations are step pyramids, which have terraced sides and a flat top, rather than smooth-sided true pyramids.
